subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Milky Way–Andromeda Collision
description: A fast breakdown of The Milky Way–Andromeda Collision for builders.

hook.text: The Milky Way and Andromeda are racing toward each other at 110 km/s. They will collide in about 4.5 billion years.

buildup.text: Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy—2.5 million light-years away and approaching. The collision is certain.

discovery.text: Simulations show the galaxies will pass through each other, swing back, and finally merge over 2 billion years.

twist.text: Individual stars will almost certainly not collide. The space between stars is too vast. Our Sun will likely survive.

climax.text: The merged galaxy, nicknamed 'Milkomeda,' will probably be a giant elliptical with no spiral arms.

punchline.text: Two galaxies on a collision course. Our Sun will probably be fine.

quiz.question: What will likely happen to our Sun during the Milky Way–Andromeda merger?
options: It will survive—the space between stars is too vast for direct collisions
It will be absorbed by Andromeda's supermassive black hole
It will be flung out of the merged galaxy entirely

details.summary: The Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies are approaching each other at about 110 km/s and will collide in roughly 4.5 billion years. Over the following 2 billion years, they'll merge into a single giant elliptical galaxy nicknamed 'Milkomeda.' Despite the collision, individual stars are so far apart…
details.whyItMatters: This upcoming merger demonstrates that galaxy evolution is ongoing — even the Milky Way's current structure is temporary. It provides a local example of the galaxy merger process that built most massive galaxies.
takeaways: Milky Way and Andromeda will collide in ~4.5 billion years
They'll merge into an elliptical galaxy called Milkomeda
Stars are too far apart for individual stellar collisions

faq.question: Will the collision destroy our solar system?
faq.answer: The Sun will have already become a red giant by then, making Earth uninhabitable. Even so, our solar system would likely survive the merger intact — stars are light-years apart and collisions are statistically negligible.

faq.question: How do we know the collision will happen?
faq.answer: Hubble Space Telescope measurements of Andromeda's sideways motion confirm it's on a near-direct collision course. The approach velocity of ~110 km/s and the 2.5 million light-year distance give a timeline of about 4.5 billion years.
